newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia stocks rebound after sharp sell-off.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia stocks rebound after sharp sell-off.

text.p: Malaysian shares rebounded on Friday, after hitting a new one-and-a-half-year low, as government-backed institutional funds supported key stocks, dealers and fund managers said.
The key Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks ended 9.09 points higher at 1,017.61 after having dipped to a low of 988.47 in morning trade.
The last time the index closed lower was December 27, 1995, when the index stood at 984.12.
"I believe there was support by government intervention," said a dealing manager at a large local brokerage.
The government-backed funds came in the afternoon and picked up selected shares to help the key index regain ground after nearly 10 days in the red.

The morning selling followed the Philippine central bank's decision to give the peso a wider trading band, viewed by many analysts as a de facto devaluation. The currency fell by 11.5 percent against the U.S. dollar after the announcement.
Nine days ago, Thailand announced a managed float of the baht following days of selling pressure on the currency. On Friday, the baht fell below 30 per dollar.
Malaysia's central Bank Negara on Wednesday warned of tough measures, including raising interest rates, to stamp out speculation in the ringgit.
It was also seen stalking the foreign exchange markets at the 2.5050 ringgit level against the greenback on Friday, threatening intervention.
Meanwhile interbank rates ballooned to 45 percent before closing at 10/15 percent, also effectively preventing shorting action on the ringgit.
"The only (undefended) loophole left to them (speculators) was the stock market," said Simon Maughan, head of research at W.I. Carr in Kuala Lumpur.
Share prices consequently plunged on short-selling activity by foreign speculators. But several factors caused a sharp rebound after the midday break.
Government-backed institutional funds were seen actively buying key index-linked stocks, including Malayan Banking Bhd, Tenaga Nasional Bhd and Telekom Malaysia Bhd.

"We're rebounding on Tun Daim's statement and a lot of local fund support," said Ang Kok Heng, general manager at TA Asset Management, referring to supportive comments on Thursday by Economic Advisor to the Government, Daim Zainuddin.
"The only way to defend the ringgit was to make the market recover," said Ramlan Ahmad, senior manager at fund managers Commerce MGI in Kuala Lumpur.
Short covering activity was also seen as speculators had to buy back stocks they had sold earlier.
Genuine interest in oversold blue chips also helped to pull the index up, analysts said, adding that next week should see a slightly steadier market.
"It will still be very volatile but I think it will not be as volatile as this week," said Ang.
"Any break below 1,000 (on the Composite Index) will be short-lived but I don't see it going above 1,050," said Maughan.
($1=2.5 ringgit)
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-206 2323)
